## Epoch 6 — complete, 12 of 12

The first epoch to finish. `qwen3.8-27b`, 3 slots x 65,536, results in
`.data/benchmark/watch/20260822-160012/`.

| task | tier | baseline | doctrine | conductor |
|------|------|----------|----------|-----------|
| slugify-ts | T0 | pass 2.0m / 52k | pass 11.0m / 352k | timeout 30m / 273k |
| euler-cli-py | T1 | pass 6.0m / 72k | pass 11.1m / 279k | timeout 45m / 372k |
| logfmt-lenses-ts | T2 | pass 5.0m / 63k | pass 17.3m / 327k | timeout 60m / 486k |
| clock-inject-py | T4 | pass 4.9m / 88k | pass 9.2m / 241k | timeout 60m / 539k |

**baseline 4/4. doctrine 4/4. conductor 0/4.** Every gauge verdict matches its outcome, so
nothing here is a scoring artefact — the two arms that finished, finished correctly.

No harness defect fired during this epoch. Nine were fixed before it, and
`scripts/check_campaign.py` finds no known signature in the results.

### The last cell answers the campaign's open question about the conductor

`conductor/clock-inject-py` is the first conductor cell in six epochs to write a **stop record**,
and what it says is the finding:

```json
{"kind": "noop",
 "reasonDisplay": "the orchestrator completed 12 consecutive turns without this run moving:
  state INTAKE, still unfinished (no item), and the phase gate's next action was
  conductor_decompose, unheeded throughout — disengaging rather than generating until the
  session ceiling ends the run with nothing on disk"}
```

Twelve consecutive turns. The phase gate named the next action every single time. The
orchestrator called it **zero** times. The disengage backstop then noticed, stopped, and wrote
down exactly what had happened.

That is D08 and D11 at full size, and it settles what has been ambiguous all campaign. The
conductor's failures are not distributed across its stages: **its stages work.** Across the six
epochs the classifier was right, the skeptic overruled the classifier and was right, the
decompose guard caught a genuinely oversized item, the decomposition on T2 produced exactly the
four disjoint items the manifest predicts, the TDD gate detected RED for the right reason, the
edit gate refused a write outside the tree, and the FSM refused every illegal transition it was
offered. Six epochs have produced no example of a conductor *judgement* being wrong.

What does not work is the orchestrator acting on what it is told. Four roles, one behaviour:

| role | told | did |
|------|------|-----|
| orchestrator | `conductor_decompose` is the next action, 12 turns running | called it zero times |
| orchestrator | `EXECUTING->DECOMPOSED` is illegal (n=3) | tried it anyway |
| planner | reply with a Plan; you may not call `conductor_plan` | called `conductor_plan` |
| planner | this item spans two clusters, here are three remedies | produced nothing for 15 minutes |

**The conductor is a system whose judgement is sound and whose steering is not.** Every
mechanism built to catch a mistake caught one. The thing none of them can do is make the model
take the action it has just been handed, and on this hardware each turn spent not taking it
costs minutes.

That is one problem, not ten, and it is upstream of every timing fix that has been considered —
a larger watchdog, a narrower reviewer fan-out and a faster classify would each buy back
minutes, and none of them would make the orchestrator call the tool the phase gate is naming.

## D26 — the state block tells the model to do one thing and how to avoid it

The steering failure is not the orchestrator ignoring instructions. It is the orchestrator
following the **last** one.

Doctrine is imperative and unambiguous (`conductor/doctrine/core.md`):

> **You do not choose the next tool from memory** — you take the recommended one; a call out
> of order is refused, not negotiated.

The live state block, rendered by `renderStateBlock` and delivered as the **final** system
append on every request, then says this:

```
Run state: INTAKE
Recommended next tool: conductor_decompose
Other legal tools available now: 4 (call conductor_status to enumerate them).
```

Two things are wrong with three lines, and they compound.

1. **"Recommended" is advisory.** It names a good option rather than the action to take. The
   doctrine's imperative sits ~13.8k tokens earlier in the same prompt; this sits last.
2. **The next line names an escape hatch.** It advertises that alternatives exist AND gives the
   exact tool to call to enumerate them — and `conductor_status` is read-only, so calling it is
   legal, advances nothing, and costs a full turn.

The intent behind that line is good and is stated in its own comment: fold the other legal tools
into a count, "never a second 'do this' that would contradict the recommendation". The count
does that. The parenthetical undoes it.

**What was observed.** Every orchestrator mismatch captured in this campaign has the same
target:

```
#2   orchestrator  rec=conductor_classify        -> conductor_status  MISMATCH
#7   orchestrator  rec=conductor_submit_test/I1  -> conductor_status  MISMATCH
#18  orchestrator  rec=conductor_vet_test/I1     -> conductor_status  MISMATCH
#21  reviewer      rec=conductor_vet_test/I1     -> conductor_status  MISMATCH
```

and the disengage backstop's summary of the T4 cell — twelve consecutive turns with
`conductor_decompose` "unheeded throughout" — is the same behaviour run to its conclusion.

**Prediction, written before the fix.** With the recommendation made imperative and the
`conductor_status` invitation removed, the per-turn capture of a conductor cell shows
`conductor_status` falling out of the mismatch column, and the mismatch rate drops below the
8-of-19 and 13-of-23 recorded so far. If the rate holds with a different tool in the mismatch
column, the diagnosis is wrong and the cause is not the block's wording.

**Held for confirmation.** Epoch 7 runs the unchanged code with D22's per-turn capture active
for the first time, so it produces the exact mismatch distribution rather than the four rows
above. The fix waits for that, because "predominantly `conductor_status`" is currently four
observations noted by eye and the campaign has already been burned twice by a claim pitched
wider than its evidence.

### Audit, continued: a doc that called live machinery dead

`docs/developer/llama-router.md` said `X-Conductor-Schema` never reaches the wire at HEAD, that
no production call site sets the flag, and that "the router-side machinery that reads it is
built, tested and **inert**, which is why every `schemaMissing` count from a real session reads
zero."

Three independent measurements say otherwise:

1. **170 of 550 ledger rows carry `schemaMissing: true`.**
2. The router writes that column **only** inside `if (observation.tagged)` (`router/router.hpp`),
   and `tagged` means the request arrived carrying `X-Conductor-Schema: required`
   (`router/schema-observer.hpp`: *"an untagged request is never missing"*).
3. `.data/configs/router.log` holds **242** of the matching warn lines:
   `carries 'X-Conductor-Schema: required' but declares no schema — counted schemaMissing (role 'mechanical', …)`.

The header reaches the wire, the observation runs, and it fires. What survives of the old claim
is its second half: those requests genuinely declare no schema in the body, which is consistent
with opencode 1.18.15 emitting no `response_format` for a prompt-shaped structured output. So
the observation is doing exactly what §4.4 built it for.

**Why this one is worth more than a typo.** A doc calling live code inert is worse than a doc
that is merely stale. It tells a reader that a signal can be ignored — and `schemaMissing` fired
242 times in one campaign, at `warn`, describing a real mismatch between what the plugin declares
and what it sends. Anyone who had read this page would have had a reason not to look. The
correction names which half is dead instead: `schemaConformed`, null on all 550 rows, which is
limit 9.

## D13 and D26 are the same defect: messages that say what not to do

Audited separately, they turn out to be one shape.

**D26 — the state block.** Says what to do, then supplies the escape:

```
Recommended next tool: conductor_decompose
Other legal tools available now: 4 (call conductor_status to enumerate them).
```

**D13 — the edit gate.** Says what is forbidden, and stops:

```
the path is outside this session's tree; an edit is confined to the tree the session was
dispatched into (§3.5), and no item scope can widen that
```

The sub-session that received this had written a test and wanted to run it and read the result:

```
node --test tests/visible.test.ts > /tmp/opencode/i1-red.log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?"; grep -E ...
```

Every part of that is what the stage is for. The only defect is the scratch path, and **nothing
in this repository tells a sub-session where scratch space is** — `grep -i 'scratch|temp file|/tmp'`
across all nine doctrine packs and `docs/developer/gates.md` returns nothing. The gate is
correct, the refusal is correct, and the model had no way to know the correct alternative, so it
lost the verification.

Both messages are precise about the rule and silent about the remedy. In a system where a turn
costs minutes, a refusal that does not name the next legal move costs a turn to discover it — and
D16's evidence is that a refused sub-session frequently discovers nothing at all before the
watchdog takes it.

**This raises the confidence in D26's fix and widens it.** The conductor's messages are unusually
good at naming the rule, the section and the measurement — the decompose guard even lists three
remedies, and that is the one refusal in the campaign that a role acted on productively. Where
they stop at the rule, the role stalls. The change is one principle applied in two places: **say
the next legal action, not only the illegal one.**

## D08 withdrawn as stated — `mismatch` counts a role doing its work

D22's per-turn capture ran on a conductor cell for the first time, and its first act was to
falsify the claim it was built to investigate. The full mismatch distribution for
`conductor/slugify-ts`, epoch 7 — 10 mismatched turns out of 35:

| what was called instead | count |
|-------------------------|------:|
| `read` | 5 |
| `conductor_status` | 2 |
| `bash` | 2 |
| `write` | 1 |

`conductor_status` is **2 of 10**, not the pattern. And the rows say why:

```
#10  testWriter  rec=conductor_submit_test/I1  -> read +2 more   MISMATCH
#11  testWriter  rec=conductor_submit_test/I1  -> bash           MISMATCH
#12  testWriter  rec=conductor_submit_test/I1  -> bash           MISMATCH
#13  testWriter  rec=conductor_submit_test/I1  -> read +1 more   MISMATCH
#14  testWriter  rec=conductor_submit_test/I1  -> write          MISMATCH
```

A testWriter reading the code, writing a test and running it, before submitting it. **That is
the stage working.** Every one of those turns is counted a mismatch, because `recommended` names
the tool that COMPLETES the stage and everything necessary to reach it is, by construction, not
that tool.

Split by role, the metric separates into two different things:

| role | turns | mismatched | rate | reading |
|------|------:|-----------:|-----:|---------|
| testWriter | 6 | 5 | 83% | doing its job — read, run, write, then submit |
| implementer | 2 | 1 | 50% | reading before marking green |
| skeptic | 2 | 1 | 50% | reading before judging |
| **orchestrator** | **8** | **3** | **38%** | **the real signal** |
| reviewer | 3 | 0 | 0% | answers directly, nothing to read |
| mechanical | 1 | 0 | 0% | answers directly |

The orchestrator is the only role whose job **is** to call the stage tool — it does no file work
— so a mismatch there is a turn spent not advancing. Every other role has to read, edit and run
before it can complete anything.

**What is withdrawn.** "The orchestrator called something other than the recommended tool on 13
of 23 turns" was a whole-run figure quoted as if it were an orchestrator figure. It was not; most
of those turns belonged to sub-sessions doing necessary work. The same error is in every earlier
`mismatches N` figure quoted from the live console in this register.

**What survives.** The orchestrator-specific version, at 3 of 8 here, and epoch 6's disengage —
twelve consecutive orchestrator turns with `conductor_decompose` unheeded — which was always
orchestrator-scoped and is unaffected.

### D26 narrowed, and still worth doing

The prediction written before the fix said: *if the rate holds with a different tool in the
mismatch column, the diagnosis is wrong.* A different tool is in the column, so the strong form
— "the model is following the `conductor_status` invitation" — is not supported.

The weak form is. `conductor_status` is still the orchestrator's most common wrong call, both of
its two occurrences are orchestrator turns, and the state block does name it as the way to see
alternatives. Fixing that is cheap and the invitation is counterproductive regardless. The
expected effect is now **two turns of a thirty-five-turn cell**, not a transformation, and the
register should say so before rather than after.

### The instrument earned its commit

D22 was added because findings were being reached by inference from a terminal that scrolled.
Its first live run overturned a claim that had been in this register for six epochs and had
already shaped a proposed fix. That is the argument for spending a commit on observability
before spending one on a remedy.

## The fix, scoped to what the evidence supports

One principle, two places: **name the next legal action, not only the illegal one.**

**D26 — `renderStateBlock` (`conductor/adapter/inject.ts`).**

```diff
- Recommended next tool: conductor_decompose
- Other legal tools available now: 4 (call conductor_status to enumerate them).
+ Next action: call conductor_decompose.
+ Other legal tools available now: 4. None of them is the next action.
```

The count stays — it is honest, and the comment defending it is right that folding alternatives
into a number avoids a second "do this". The instruction that followed it does not stay: it named
a read-only tool that advances nothing, in the line immediately after the one naming the action
that does.

One deliberate exception: `renderNoRunStateBlock` still names `conductor_status`, and that is not
the D26 case — with no live run there is no next action for it to compete with, so pointing at
the one tool that can report what the workspace holds is the whole of the useful advice.

**D13 — the edit gate's out-of-tree refusal (`conductor/core/gates-edit.ts`).** The rule is
unchanged; the remedy is added:

```
… and no item scope can widen that. Write it under /work/repo instead — scratch files
included, and a path relative to that tree is always inside it
```

**Tests, both verified red first.** `[D13] an out-of-tree edit is refused with the tree it may
write under` pins that the refusal names the tree AND covers scratch explicitly, since a session
reaching for `/tmp` is not looking for a source path. In `inject-wiring.test.ts`, two assertions
pin that a block naming an action does not also instruct the session to call `conductor_status`,
and that the count survives — so a future edit cannot restore the invitation by restoring the
count.

**Expected effect, stated before the run rather than after.** Two turns of a thirty-five-turn
cell for D26, on the evidence above. D13's is unmeasured: it fired once in seven epochs, and its
cost when it fires is a lost verification rather than a lost turn. Neither is the thing that
makes the conductor miss its budgets — that is D16, the planner's sub-session not fitting a
900-second watchdog — and this register should not let a cheap fix that was easy to reason about
stand in for the expensive one that was not.

**Held for a clean gate.** Epoch 7 is running, and D24 says a gate run beside a benchmark is not
a gate. The change is committed after it finishes.

## The before-fix baseline, from two captured conductor cells

Both epoch-7 conductor cells carried D22's per-turn capture. Their numbers are the control the
three staged fixes get judged against, recorded before any of them lands.

**`conductor/slugify-ts` (T0, 35 turns)** and **`conductor/euler-cli-py` (T1, 33 turns)**:

| role | turns (T0 / T1) | mismatched | reading |
|------|-----------------|-----------:|---------|
| planner | — / **15** | 10 | the biggest consumer of turns in the system |
| orchestrator | 8 / 10 | 3 / 5 | the only role whose job IS to call the stage tool |
| testWriter | 6 / — | 5 | read, run, write, then submit — the stage working |
| skeptic | 2 / 5 | 1 / 3 | reads before judging |
| reviewer | 3 / — | 0 | answers directly |
| mechanical | 1 / 3 | 0 / 2 | answers directly |

### D26 weakens again, and the honest number is now 3 of 8

Orchestrator mismatch targets, both cells pooled:

| called instead | count |
|----------------|------:|
| `read` | 5 |
| `conductor_status` | 3 |

`conductor_status` is **3 of 8 orchestrator mismatches**, not the pattern even within the role
the metric is meaningful for. The orchestrator's most common wrong call is **reading files**.

That is the second downward revision of D26 in one session. The first, from the T0 capture, cut
"the model is following the invitation" to "two turns of thirty-five". This one says that even
among orchestrator turns — the only ones that count — the invitation explains a minority. The
change is still worth making: the line is counterproductive on its own terms, and removing it
cannot cost anything. But the register should be plain that **it is now expected to move almost
nothing**, and that a fix surviving two rounds of shrinking evidence is a fix looking for a
justification.

What the `read` majority actually suggests is a different, untested hypothesis: the orchestrator
reaches for repository context the state block does not give it, and the block names an action
without naming what the run is about. That is worth measuring before it is worth fixing.

### D16's root: the planner takes fifteen turns

The T1 cell recorded **1 watchdog kill** and shows why. The planner took **15 turns** — more than
any other role, more than the orchestrator's 10 — and the ledger has planner turns running to
451 seconds. Fifteen turns of a role like that cannot fit a 900-second sub-session budget under
any watchdog value that is not larger than the cell budget itself.

So D16 is not "the planner hangs" and it is not "the watchdog is too short". It is **the planner
needs fifteen turns to answer**, and every remedy that does not reduce that number moves the
failure rather than removing it. That is the expensive problem this campaign has identified and
has not yet touched, and none of the three staged fixes addresses it.

## D29 — the orchestrator reads instead of advancing

Three conductor cells now carry per-turn capture. Pooling their orchestrator turns — the only
role for which `mismatch` means anything, since the orchestrator does no file work of its own:

| called instead of the stage tool | count | share |
|----------------------------------|------:|------:|
| `read` | 11 | **61%** |
| `conductor_status` | 5 | 28% |
| `bash` | 2 | 11% |

**The orchestrator's dominant wrong move is reading the repository.** Not polling status, not
calling an illegal tool — reading files, on a role whose entire job is to call the tool the phase
gate has just named.

The disengage backstop has now fired twice, and its two reasons are the same sentence with the
nouns changed:

```
epoch 6, T4:  12 consecutive turns without this run moving: state INTAKE,
              ... the phase gate's next action was conductor_decompose, unheeded throughout

epoch 7, T2:  12 consecutive turns without this run moving: state DECOMPOSED,
              still unfinished by-status-lens (PENDING), errors-lens (PENDING),
              latency-lens (PENDING), slowest-lens (PENDING),
              ... the phase gate's next action was conductor_plan, unheeded throughout
```

The second one is the sharper of the two. The decomposition had **succeeded** — four disjoint
items, exactly the trajectory the manifest predicts for that task — and the orchestrator then
spent twelve turns reading files rather than calling `conductor_plan` on them. It also took **17
turns** in that cell, more than the planner's 14: the orchestrator is not merely failing to
advance, it is the single largest consumer of turns in the run.

### What this does to D26

D26 explains **5 of 18**. It is staged, it is cheap, and the invitation it removes is
counterproductive on its own terms — but three captures in, the honest summary is that it
addresses a quarter of the behaviour and the register has said so at each shrink rather than
after the fact.

### The hypothesis D29 actually suggests, and why it is not yet a fix

The state block tells the orchestrator **what state the run is in** and **what tool to call
next**. It does not tell it what the run is *about*: no prompt, no item titles, no file scopes —
`renderStateBlock` deliberately "names only the single recommended tool … never the full item
list, so it stays bounded no matter how many items the run carries", and that boundedness is a
real property worth keeping.

So a plausible reading of eleven reads is a role trying to recover context it is not given,
before committing to an action it cannot take back. That is a hypothesis with an obvious test —
add the item titles and their file scopes to the block for the orchestrator, bounded by a cap,
and see whether the read count falls — and it is **not** yet supported. It is one explanation of
a correlation, the campaign has been wrong three times this way already, and the last one was
this same defect. It goes in the register as a question, not a change.

### What epoch 7 added that epoch 6 could not

Epoch 6 produced the same scoreboard and could not explain it. Epoch 7 carried the per-turn
capture, and the explanation is now measured rather than inferred:

- **D29 established (n=3 cells)** — the orchestrator's dominant wrong move is `read`, 11 of 18,

**why**, and every one of those four statements came from an instrument added between them.

### Audit: a previously-falsified claim, checked rather than assumed

`docs/developer/doctrine-system.md` says the pack selection is "de-duplicated, so a pack already
in the role's row is never appended twice". The 13.2 register lists that sentence as falsified by
finding F02 — `core.md` reaching the model twice per orchestrator request.

**It is accurate today, and the audit's job was to find that out rather than assume either way.**
The F02 fix landed: `conductor/opencode-fragment.json` carries a 147-character pointer where it
once carried the pack, and `conductor/tests/fragment.test.ts` pins that with a comment naming the
13.2 measurement. Claim falsified, fix shipped, test added to hold it — the loop this campaign
keeps arguing for, already closed by a previous one.

What was worth adding is the half the page did not explain. The de-duplication was never wrong;
it covered the plugin's append list and did so correctly, and the duplicate arrived through a
second channel the list cannot see. A reader of this page alone would take "never twice" as a
property of the system when it is a property of one mechanism plus a separate decision about the
agent prompt. Both halves are now named, with the test that holds the second.

**The generalisable bit:** F02 was not a de-duplication bug. It was a component behaving
correctly over the inputs it was given, in a system where something else supplied the same input
by another route. Auditing the component would never have found it; only counting what the model
actually received did.

## D30 — a fix of mine that cost a turn in the very next run

Epoch 8's `conductor/slugify-ts` never reached the vet wave, so D27 went untested. It exposed
something worth more.

```
25.9m  DENY  cat > /tmp/opencode/classify.json      <- the original D13 case
             "… Write it under /Users/sal/.llama-leash-work/… — scratch files
              included, and a path relative to that tree is always inside it"
26.4m  DENY  cat > .classify-check.json             <- it FOLLOWED that advice
             "the path is outside this session's tree …"
```

**The advice was the exact opposite of the truth.** `normalizeUnderTree` matches the tree as a
string PREFIX (`absPath.startsWith(tree + "/")`), so a relative name never starts with it and is
always denied. The classifier read the remedy, rewrote its redirect, and was refused a second
time. The message turned one lost turn into two on a machine where a turn is minutes.

The function is four lines long and its parameter is named `absPath`. It was never opened. The
sentence was written from a mental model of how path resolution ought to work — in the same
commit that corrected three other pages for asserting things their authors had not verified.

**The corrected message** names the spelling the check accepts rather than a location alone, and
promises nothing about writability, since an item's `fileScope` still applies on top:

```
… Paths are matched as absolute paths under <tree> — a bare or relative name is not
resolved against it, so spell the whole path (an item's fileScope still applies on top of this)
```

**The corrected test is the part that generalises.** It no longer checks the wording against a
reading of the wording. It checks the remedy against the gate:

- a relative path must still `deny` — *"if this ever starts passing, the message above is wrong
  again and needs rewriting with it"*
- an absolute in-scope path must not
- the message must never again contain a promise that relative works

Checking prose against prose is what produced the defect. Checking prose against the function is
the only thing that would have caught it.

### The rest of that cell, and what it means for D27

Three known defects recurred in the same thirty minutes:

- **D16 at a new site.** The *skeptic* hit the fifteen-minute watchdog — previously only the
  planner. Half the cell's budget, gone before classification finished.
- **D10, n=2.** The classifier emitted unparseable JSON again.
- **A guard escalation that may block D27 entirely.** After all of the above, the classify guard
  rejected the trivial item and escalated the run to `work`:

  ```
  guard-reject classify escalate-to-work
    item "I1" is too large: its acceptance spans 2 clusters (src/slugify.ts, export),
    over the one-cluster item budget
  ```

  This is D25's one-cluster budget again, now firing on a **four-line string function**. If
  `slugify-ts` escalates to `work`, the trivial path never runs and D27's one-critic narrowing
  never applies. **D27 may be unmeasurable until D25 is resolved**, which makes the open question
  in D25 — is the one-cluster budget too strict, or is the manifest's expectation wrong — the
  next thing worth deciding rather than the next thing worth coding.

## D25 withdrawn — the guard was right and this repository already said so

D25 was recorded as a disagreement between two parts of the repository: the one-cluster item
budget refusing the single item `euler-cli-py`'s expected trajectory calls for, and later
refusing to let a four-line string function stay trivial. It was written up as needing a
decision — loosen the budget, or fix the manifest.

Neither. `docs/build/artifacts/acceptance-cluster-defect.md` is 553 lines about this exact rule,
and it settles it.

**The rule.** The plan states it once — `item size (scope > ~5 files or > 1 acceptance cluster)`
— and never defines *cluster*. The implementation approximates a criterion's subject as its
first non-determiner token. It is also the **only** acceptance-size check the trivial route
passes through, since that route skips the plan-review lens entirely, so deleting it would leave
trivial items unchecked for size.

**Why it misfires.** A token's position in an English sentence is not its subject:

```
· slugify lowercases the input
· leading hyphens are removed        -> ["slugify", "leading"]   2 clusters, REJECT
```

Both criteria describe one function in one file. `leading` names nothing. That is exactly the
campaign's two sightings — `(src.cli.main, fresh)` and `(src/slugify.ts, export)`.

**Why it is not an open question.** The rule has been repaired twice, and §8 of that artifact —
titled *What it still wrongly refuses* — lists verb-leading and abstaining criteria as the known,
accepted residual. The documented remedy is not a looser budget: it is that the planner open each
criterion with what it is about (`parse rejects empty input`, not `rejects empty input`), which
the generated mechanics block already instructs it to do.

So the guard is working as written and as documented, and **the planner is not following an
instruction it has been given.** That is D29's family, not a design conflict, and D25 folds into
it.

### The bias that produced it, which is the reusable part

§5 of that artifact records the 13.2 campaign hitting this same refusal, quoting the journal
accurately, and concluding it was "the ONE ACCEPTANCE AUTHORITY design working exactly as
written". That was wrong, and the artifact explains why it was easy to write:

> **A refusal is the shape of a guard working.** The campaign was hunting for defects that let
> bad things THROUGH ... Against that lens a refusal reads as the control group.

This campaign made the mirror-image error against the same evidence. Hunting for over-strict
machinery in an arm that never finishes, a refusal read as the machinery being over-strict.
**Same journal line, opposite prior, both wrong** — and the correct reading had been written
down, in this repository, before either of us looked.

The cheap defence is not a better prior. It is `grep -ril cluster docs/build/artifacts/` before
theorising about a guard, because a repository that has been audited before has usually already
argued with itself about the thing you just noticed.

## D31 — an unlisted preservation shape, reproduced and deliberately left alone

Withdrawing D25 left a loose end: the guard is correct, but *why* did it count two clusters on a
four-line function? The captured snapshot from epoch 8 has the classifier's actual acceptance,
and the refusal reproduces byte-for-byte off a bare `node` import:

```
clusters: ["src/slugify.ts","export"]  count = 2

  ["src/slugify.ts"]  <- slugify('Hello, World!') returns 'hello-world'
  ["src/slugify.ts"]  <- slugify('  --Foo__Bar--  ') returns 'foo-bar'
  ["src/slugify.ts"]  <- slugify('a1 b2') returns 'a1-b2'
  ["src/slugify.ts"]  <- slugify('Hello') returns 'hello' and the existing test … keeps passing
  ["export"]          <- The export remains export function slugify(input: string): string
```

Four criteria fold onto the declared file. The fifth is a **preservation** criterion, and the
repair's own principle is that a criterion which preserves rather than delivers contributes
none. It is not recognised because `PRESERVATION_CLAIMS` requires the verb to be followed by a
closed set of sameness words:

```
(?:is|are|was|were|stays?|remains?)\s+(?:unchanged|unmodified|untouched|unaffected|intact|the\s+same|as\s+before|byte-for-byte)
```

`remains export function slugify(input: string): string` preserves by **restating the value**
rather than by naming sameness. Neither §7 ("What it does not catch") nor §8 ("What it still
wrongly refuses") lists that shape.

### Why this is recorded and not fixed

The obvious patch is to widen the preservation verb to accept any object. Three reasons not to
reach for it here:

1. **The artifact already reasoned about widening.** §7: *"The abstention grammar is itself
   learnable. Whatever makes a criterion uncounted is a rule a planner can follow to stop being
   counted."* Every loosening is also an escape hatch, and that page weighed each one against
   the teeth rows it had to keep.
2. **The documented remedy already works.** Run through the same function, subject-first phrasing
   collapses to one cluster: `slugify keeps its export name and signature` -> `["src/slugify.ts"]`.
   The generated mechanics block already instructs the planner to open a criterion with what it
   is about. This is the same instruction-not-followed shape as D29.
3. **The campaign has been wrong three times acting on a five-minute reading of something this
   repository had already analysed at length** — most recently D25, one hour before this. A
   553-line artifact with a rate-guarded regression corpus is exactly the kind of prior work that
   should be *added to* by its author, not patched around by a passer-by holding one new example.

What this campaign contributes is the example: a reproduction, a byte-identical repro off a bare
import, and the observation that it is the shape that blocks the trivial route on the cheapest
task in the ladder. That is worth more to whoever rewrites §8 than a regex edit made without the
corpus in view.

**Consequence for D27, stated plainly:** the one-critic narrowing is gated behind a `trivial`
classification, `slugify-ts` escalates to `work` on this shape, and so **D27 remains unmeasured
and will stay so until either the planner phrases criteria subject-first or this shape is
recognised.** Neither has happened, and the register should not carry D27 as though the next
epoch will settle it.

## Epoch 9's T0 conductor cell — one prediction held, one failed, one untestable

```
 1.7m   classify   2.9 min  -> trivial
 4.6m   skeptic    3.0 min  -> agreed
        guard-reject classify escalate-to-work
          item "I1" is too large: its acceptance spans 2 clusters (src/slugify.ts, export)
        -> INTAKE work -> DECOMPOSED
 8.2m   planner   10.0 min
18.5m   planner   UNFINISHED
30.0m   wall clock expires
```

**D31 held, at n=2, byte-identical.** Same two clusters, same escalation, same four-line string
function pushed off the trivial route. The prediction written when D31 was recorded — that this
shape blocks the trivial route on the cheapest task in the ladder — is now observed twice.

**D27 remains unmeasurable, exactly as stated in advance.** The run never classified trivial, so
the one-critic narrowing never applied. This was written down before the epoch rather than after
it, which is the only reason it is not a disappointment.

### D26's prediction is falsified

The prediction, recorded before the change shipped:

> With the recommendation made imperative and the `conductor_status` invitation removed, the
> per-turn capture of a conductor cell shows `conductor_status` falling out of the mismatch
> column.

It did not. Orchestrator mismatches this cell: `conductor_status` **2**, `read` 1.

| | orchestrator mismatches | of which `conductor_status` |
|---|---|---|
| before D26 (3 cells) | 18 | 5 |
| after D26 (1 cell) | 3 | 2 |

Three mismatched turns is far too few to claim the share rose. What can be claimed is the thing
the prediction ruled on: **the calls did not stop.** The block no longer names `conductor_status`
anywhere, and the orchestrator called it anyway — so the invitation was not the cause, and the
sentence that removing it "cannot cost anything" was true while "it addresses a quarter of the
behaviour" was not.

D26 shrank from "the pattern" to "5 of 18" to "not the cause" across three measurements, each
recorded when it happened. The change stays — an imperative next action and no advertised escape
is better writing regardless — but it is now shipped with **no observed effect**, and the
register says that rather than leaving a plausible story standing.

**D30 was not exercised.** No `deny` fired in this cell, so the corrected refusal text has still
never been read by a model. It remains untested in the only way that matters.

### What did move, and what it does not explain

Turn counts fell sharply: orchestrator 7 (was 8, 10, 17), planner 8 (was 14, 15). And the cell
still burned its full thirty minutes, because two planner waves at 10.0 minutes and 11.5 minutes
account for most of it. **Fewer turns did not help, because the cost is per-turn wall clock, not
turn count** — which is D16 restated, and nothing shipped touches D16.

## D32 — the block told a sub-session to call a tool the gate refuses it for

The per-turn capture, byte-exact, epoch 9:

```
#9  planner  rec=conductor_decompose  ->  conductor_decompose  REFUSED
    "conductor_decompose is not among the tools such a session may call.
     A sub-session may call: conductor_override, conductor_status, conductor_surface (§3.5)"
```

**The planner did exactly what the state block told it to do, and was refused for it.**

`legalTools(run, items, questions, repoConfigured, publishEnabled)` takes **no role parameter**.
It answers "where does the RUN go next" — a question about the run. `renderStateBlock` shows that
answer to every session that reads a block, sub-sessions included, and §3.5 lets a sub-session
call only `conductor_override`, `conductor_status`, `conductor_surface`. The block already
carries the role on `SessionRegistryEntry`; it simply never consulted it.

### This inverts D15, and D15's family

D15 was recorded as *"the planner sub-session calls `conductor_plan` — a tool its role may not
call — instead of replying with the Plan"*, and filed alongside D11 and D29 as the orchestrator
family: roles ignoring what they are told. **It is the opposite.** The planner was obeying, and
the instruction was wrong for it.

That is the third time this campaign a refusal in the journal has been read as the guarded
party's fault:

| | read as | actually |
|---|---|---|
| D08 | the orchestrator ignoring the recommended tool | a metric counting a role doing its job |
| D25 | the cluster guard being too strict | the guard correct, already documented, planner phrasing |
| D15/D32 | the planner reaching for a forbidden tool | the block handing it one |

**A guard firing looks like the guarded party's fault.** It is the campaign's most repeated
diagnostic error and the only thing that has reliably caught it is the per-turn capture showing
what was RECOMMENDED beside what was CALLED — a column that did not exist before D22.

### The fix

A sub-session whose role cannot call the run's stage tool is told what it should do instead:

```
Next action: reply with your result. The run's next step is conductor_decompose, which the
orchestrator takes from your reply — a sub-session may call only conductor_override,
conductor_status, conductor_surface (§3.5).
```

The allow-list is `callableBy(kind)`, added to `core/tool-legality.ts` and derived from the same
`TOOL_LEGALITY` table `callerAllowed` builds its refusal from, so the block cannot name a set the
gate disagrees with. The test asserts both directions: every tool the block names is one
`callerAllowed` permits, and every tool `callerAllowed` permits is named. Verified red-first;
`core` purity intact.

**Prediction, and it is structural rather than statistical.** Unlike D26 — which predicted a
frequency and was falsified — this predicts an impossibility: `rec=<stage tool> -> <stage tool>
REFUSED` from a sub-session role cannot appear in a per-turn capture again, because the block can
no longer emit that recommendation to that role. One occurrence falsifies it.

**Epoch 9 stopped early.** Its remaining cells would have measured D26, already falsified, and
D30, never exercised. D32 is the first fix in this campaign with a mechanism rather than a
correlation, and measuring it is worth more than finishing a run whose open questions have
already closed.
